text: This lab is where the last three lessons come together into practice. You'll verify two real quantum gates and compute the eigenvalues of a genuinely complex Hermitian matrix, using the conjugate, transpose, at-sign, allclose, and eigenvalue tools introduced so far.

Four tasks. Verify Pauli-Y is unitary, end to end. Verify the S-gate is unitary but deliberately fails the Hermitian check. Work out the eigenvalues of a complex Hermitian matrix by hand with trace and determinant, then confirm with np dot linalg dot eigvalsh. And see why a Hermitian matrix's eigenvalues always come out real, no matter how many complex entries it contains off the diagonal.

is_unitary of Y returns True, reproducing the Lesson 11 result directly. For the S-gate, diagonal one and j, is_unitary also returns True, but is_hermitian returns False, because S has j in its bottom-right corner while its conjugate transpose has negative j there. This is your working proof, in code, that a gate being unitary says nothing about whether it's also Hermitian.

Matrix A has off-diagonal entries one plus j and one minus j, conjugates of each other, and real diagonal entries two and three, so is_hermitian returns True. By hand: trace equals five, determinant equals four, and solving the quadratic gives eigenvalues four and one. np dot linalg dot eigvalsh confirms exactly that, one and four, with no stray plus-zero-j residue at all, because every Hermitian matrix guarantees real eigenvalues by construction.
Chapter 4 turns these numbers into pictures: Matplotlib fundamentals for scientific plots, building toward probability histograms and a Bloch sphere visualization of a qubit state.
